# Practical considerations

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## When the fit goes wrong

### The optimiser does not converge

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
Usually one of four things:

- the starting values are far from any reasonable fit, so the search walks off into parameter values where the model breaks
- the likelihood is flat in some direction, so there is no slope to follow
- the parameters live on wildly different scales, as $\beta$ and $\gamma$ did today
- the optimiser has hit a bound, or has no bound where it needed one
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The estimates cannot be pinned down

- Several parameter combinations fit equally well, so the answer depends on where you started
- Two parameters are strongly correlated and only their ratio is determined, as with $\beta$ and $\gamma$
- There simply are not enough data for the number of parameters you are trying to estimate

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### What to try

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- Start from several different places and check that they agree
- Look at the profile likelihood or the posterior for each parameter, not just the point estimate
- Fix a parameter you know from elsewhere, or put a prior on it
- Bring in another kind of data that speaks to the parameter the outbreak curve cannot
- Simplify the model until it is identifiable, then add complexity back one piece at a time
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The estimates converge, but they are nonsense

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- Check the model's assumptions against what you know about the disease and the setting
- Check the data: reporting changes, backfilled counts, a definition that changed halfway through
- Plot the residuals over time; a pattern in them is the model telling you what it is missing
- See how much the estimates move when you change something you were unsure about
- Fit a different model and compare
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Habits that save time

### Before fitting

- Plot the data and understand how they were collected
- Decide what you believe about each parameter before the data tell you, and write it down as bounds or priors
- Prepare several starting values

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### While fitting

- Watch the optimiser or the chain, rather than only reading the final number
- Check that different starts land in the same place
- Keep a record of every fit, including the ones that failed

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### After fitting

- Plot the fit over the data, with its uncertainty
- Report intervals, not just estimates
- See what happens to the conclusions when the assumptions change
- If the model will be used to predict, test it on data it has not seen

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Software

### R packages

-   [`bbmle`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bbmle/vignettes/mle.pdf): maximum likelihood, profiles and confidence intervals, as used today
-   [`rstan`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/rstan.pdf) and [`cmdstanr`](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/): Stan from R
-   [`pomp`](https://kingaa.github.io/pomp/vignettes/getting_started.html): particle filtering and particle MCMC
-   [`brms`](https://paul-buerkner.github.io/brms/index.html): Bayesian regression models with Stan underneath
-   [`nimble`](https://r-nimble.org/): Bayesian models with your own choice of MCMC algorithm

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Beyond R

-   [`Stan`](https://mc-stan.org): the probabilistic programming language behind `rstan`, `cmdstanr` and `brms`
-   [`OpenBUGS`](https://sourceforge.net/p/openbugs/wiki/Home/) and [`JAGS`](https://mcmc-jags.sourceforge.io): the older generation of Gibbs samplers, still widely used
-   [`PyMC`](https://www.pymc.io/welcome.html): Bayesian inference in Python
-   [`Turing.jl`](https://turinglang.org/): Bayesian inference in Julia
